papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of a Hamming quantum kernel (a Hamming-weight-weighted post-processing of the fidelity-kernel measurement statistics) for SVM classification of PCA-reduced MNIST and synthetic quantum-circuit data with 2 to 27 qubits.

existing.note: Value matches the abstract. Thresholds differ inside the paper: the abstract says 15 or more qubits, the introduction and conclusion say greater than 15, the 0/6 text says the FQK drops for n of at least 15, and on odd/even FQK is comparable to HQK up to 13 qubits. On the quantum dataset the text says HQK beats FQK for all qubit counts.

assertions.value: The authors define the Hamming quantum kernel as a sum over measured bitstrings b of the probability of obtaining b, weighted by an exponential factor in the Hamming weight h(b) with the hyperparameter λ.
quotes: Specifically, we group measurement outcomes (bitstrings) by their Hamming weight and assign a weight to each group, modulating its influence on the kernel value:
κHQK (xi, xj ) = |⟨b|U †(xi)U (xj )|0⟩⊗n|2e−λh(b) .
Here, h(b) is the Hamming weight of the bitstring b, and λ is a hyperparameter.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the kernel in Section III, Eq. (6).
assertions.reader_inference: The weight is e raised to minus lambda times the Hamming weight, so the all-zero bitstring has weight 1 and every other bitstring is discounted; the sum over b was printed on its own line in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel matrix has all entries equal to 1 when λ is 0 and converges asymptotically to the fidelity quantum kernel as λ goes to infinity.
quotes: The kernel matrix κHQK will have entries all equal to 1 when λ = 0 and asymptotically converges to the fidelitybased quantum kernel KFQK, see Eq. (4), as λ → ∞.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation in the paper; it follows from Eq. (6).
assertions.reader_inference: Immediate from Eq. (6), so the FQK is the large-λ limit of the HQK; this is why the paper treats the FQK as a special case of HQK in its hyperparameter sweeps.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming weighting ensures the similarity measure between different data points does not decrease to zero as the system size increases.
quotes: This method ensures that, as the system size increases, the similarity metric between different data points will not decrease to zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: No theorem or bound accompanies the statement. Entries of Eq. (6) stay near 1 for small λ by construction, which says nothing yet about whether differences between same-class and different-class entries stay resolvable with a finite number of shots; the paper's evidence for that is test accuracy only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel is a classical post-processing method based on the same measurement outcomes as the fidelity quantum kernel, and that it avoids the exponential concentration problem by using the full measurement statistics rather than a single fidelity value.
quotes: We introduce the Hamming quantum kernel, a classical post-processing method that is based on the same measurement outcomes as the fidelity quantum kernel.
However, it avoids the exponential concentration problem by using the full measurement statistics rather than a single fidelity value.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper never measures kernel-entry variance or concentration directly; avoidance is inferred from test accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel rests on the heuristic that similar datapoints on average lead to bitstrings of low Hamming weight, and report in the method figure that the Hamming distributions for same-class and different-class pairs stay distinctly shifted at larger qubit numbers.
quotes: Instead, we use the additional heuristic that similar datapoints on average lead to bitstrings of low Hamming weight.
However, the Hamming distributions are still distinctly shifted, allowing for an efficient classification.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: The shifted distributions are shown only in Fig. 1(c) and (d) for MNIST 0 versus 6 at n equal to 4 and 27; no numbers are in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 8, that fidelity quantum kernel entries exponentially concentrate with increasing system size, driving the kernel matrix toward the identity and yielding near-random performance, and that under a polynomial shot budget this can leave a model insensitive to the input data.
quotes: FQK for QSVM suffers from a major downside: kernel entries exponentially concentrate with increasing system size [8], driving the kernel matrix toward the identity and yielding near-random performance.
Under a polynomial shot budget, this can result in a model that is largely insensitive to the input data and exhibits poor generalization performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 8 (Thanasilp et al.).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 8, that a quantity exhibits exponential concentration in the number of qubits n if the probability that it deviates from its mean by a small amount is exponentially small, and that for kernels this means all non-diagonal entries converge to 0 exponentially fast with high probability as n increases.
quotes: The quantity X(α) is said to exhibit exponential concentration in the number of qubits n if the probability that it deviates from µ by a small amount δ is exponentially small.
which in practice means that all non-diagonal entries converge to 0 exponentially fast with high probability as the number of qubits n increases,
FQK for QSVM suffers from a major downside: kernel entries exponentially concentrate with increasing system size [8], driving the kernel matrix toward the identity
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper attributes to Ref. 8.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming the feature vectors are randomly chosen n-qubit quantum states, their overlap scales roughly as 2 to the power of minus n, which would need an exponential number of measurements to distinguish it from 0.
quotes: Assuming that the feature vectors are randomly chosen n-qubit quantum states, their overlap scales like ∼ 2−n, which would require an exponential number of measurements to distinguish them from 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: A standard Haar-random argument given without derivation; the ZZ feature map actually used is not Haar random, so the statement is a motivation, not a property shown for the circuits simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that all quantum kernels use the ZZ feature map applied three times (m = 3), with each datapoint scaled between 0 and 2π before encoding.
assertions.anchor: Section II A 2, Eq. (3), p.3 and p.4
quotes: Every datapoint xi is scaled between 0 and 2π before being encoded onto the feature map.
In this work, the feature map is applied three times(m = 3), re-uploading the data through three successive layers of the circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section II A 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that no kernel alignment is performed for any dataset and that the ZZ kernel of Eq. (3) is used as introduced.
assertions.anchor: Section II A p.4; Section VI p.11
quotes: In this work, we will therefore not apply kernel alignment and use the ZZ-kernel as introduced in Eq. [3].
No kernel alignment is performed for any dataset, making the HQK extraction process both problem-agnostic and efficient.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section II A and Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: The FQK baseline is therefore a fixed ZZ map with no bandwidth scaling, while the HQK gets one tuned hyperparameter; the paper itself cites bandwidth tuning as important for FQKs (Refs. 6 and 11).

assertions.value: The authors state that they compute only the upper triangular part of each kernel matrix and set the lower triangle by symmetry, which does not guarantee positive semidefiniteness, and that projection onto the nearest positive semidefinite matrix replaces negative eigenvalues by 0.
quotes: we construct only the upper triangular part of the kernel matrix and define the lower triangle by symmetry, i.e., K(i, j) = K(j, i).
Although this enforces symmetry, it does not guarantee positive semidefiniteness.
The projection is realized by eigendecomposing the matrix and replacing its negative eigenvalues by 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own procedure in Section II A 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the projection onto a positive semidefinite matrix is used for system sizes below 10 qubits for both quantum kernels, and that systems exceeding 10 qubits satisfy the positive semidefinite condition without it.
quotes: The same procedure to guarantee positive semidefinitness of the quantum kernel for system size less than 10 will also be used later for our Hamming quantum kernel (See Sec. III) as the systems exceeding 10 qubits satisfy the PSD condition without the need of this procedure.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as an observation with no data or proof. The paper gives no argument that the HQK of Eq. (6) is positive semidefinite in general.

assertions.value: The authors state that expectation values used for the quantum kernel elements are always calculated over 1024 shots, independently of the number of qubits.
quotes: Expectation values utilized for determining quantum kernel elements are always calculated over 1024 shots (independently of the number of qubits).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section IV B.
assertions.reader_inference: A fixed shot count means the FQK's collapse at larger n is partly a finite-shot effect; the paper does not rerun with more shots.

assertions.value: The authors report that the HQK accuracy on the quantum dataset stays close to the theoretical maximum given by the distinguishability.
quotes: In addition, the HQK accuracy stays close to the theoretical maximum given by the distinguishability.
Notably, the HQK not only surpasses both the FQK and RBF kernel in test accuracy, but also achieves performance close to the theoretical maximum.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that the HQK provides a clear advantage in test accuracy over the FQK for qubit counts greater than 15 on both classical and quantum datasets, and that the HQK is a strong candidate to replace the FQK in large-scale settings or when computational resources are limited.
quotes: The Hamming quantum kernel (HQK) provides a clear advantage in test accuracy over the standard fidelity quantum kernel (FQK) for qubit counts greater than 15 on both classical and quantum datasets.
Our empirical results indicate that the HQK is a strong candidate to replace the FQK in large-scale settings or when computational resources are limited.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: Evidence is simulation with 1024 shots, five runs, 100 training points and an FQK without bandwidth tuning; the comparison to a tuned FQK or to projected kernels is not run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results demonstrate that the Hamming quantum kernel improves the expressivity and robustness at larger qubit scales without requiring any additional quantum resources.
quotes: This demonstrates that the Hamming quantum kernel improves the expressivity and robustness at larger qubit scales without requiring any additional quantum ressources.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: Expressivity is not measured; only test accuracy is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state three open directions: a general framework for finding efficient distribution-informed classical post-processing functions, understanding the HQK accuracy difference between the odd versus even task and the 0 versus 6 task, and understanding the factors that govern HQK performance across diverse quantum circuits.
quotes: The first and most fundamental direction is the development of a general framework for finding efficient distribution-informed classical post-processing functions
A second direction concerns the MNIST dataset: in particular, understanding the difference in accuracy achieved by the HQK between the odd/even task and the 0/6 task
A third exciting direction stems from the strong performance of the HQK on quantum datasets
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its open problems in Section VI.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 7, that early investigations show fidelity quantum kernels can solve problems classical computers cannot efficiently address, but only for highly specialized problems, and that this needs a FASQ quantum computer because it relies on Shor-type data encoding.
quotes: Early investigations of fidelity quantum kernels demonstrate that they can, in
principle, solve problems that cannot be efficiently addressed by classical computers [7].

However, this has only been demonstrated for highly specialized problems with structures that quantum computers can leverage, and it necessitates a FASQ quantum computer because it relies on Shor-type data encoding.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 7 (Liu, Arunachalam and Temme).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 11, that numerical results suggest fidelity quantum kernels show no clear quantum advantage on classical data, and that tuning the kernel bandwidth improves performance but makes the kernels easier to simulate classically.
quotes: Ref. [11] presents numerical results suggesting that fidelity quantum kernels (FQKs) do not show a clear quantum advantage when applied to classical data
However, this also makes the kernels easier to simulate classically, due to unfavorable geometric difference values [10], which reduces the potential quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 11 (Slattery et al.).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 10, that projected quantum kernels address concentration by computing the inner product between low-dimensional approximations of the state, which limits the ability to capture high-order correlations between data points.
quotes: A solution to this problem was proposed by projected quantum kernels [10], where the inner product is calculated between low-dimensional approximations of the state.
However, this approach limits the ability to capture high-order correlations between data points, making it potentially unsuitable for certain datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 10 (Huang et al.).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 5, that on a breast cancer dataset of 536 samples a classical SVM achieved a test accuracy of 90%, outperforming a QSVM by 5 percentage points.
quotes: The evaluation was performed on a dataset of 536 samples.
Classical SVM achieved a test accuracy of 90%, outperforming QSVM by 5 percentage points.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 5 (Saini et al.).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 6, that a systematic comparison of more than 20,000 models found hyperparameters, particularly regularization and bandwidth tuning, critical for effective training of kernels.
quotes: A systematic comparison of more than 20,000 models to investigate the impact of various hyperparameters on kernel accuracy is carried out in [6].
A key finding of the study emphasizes the critical role of hyperparameters, particularly regularization and bandwidth tuning, in ensuring the effective training of kernels.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 6 (Schnabel and Roth).

assertions.value: The authors state that the use of Hamming weights for error mitigation in quantum kernels was first introduced in Ref. 12, and that their own approach differs in how the Hamming weight information enters the post-processing, using all measured bitstrings with a weight instead of a few bitstrings close to the all-zero bitstring.
assertions.anchor: Section I p.2; Section III p.5
quotes: the use of Hamming weights for error mitigation in quantum kernels was first introduced in [12].

By relying on all measured bitstrings, discounted by an appropriate weight, instead of only few, selected bitstrings close to the all-zero bitstring, our approach can seamlessly deal with different problems and system sizes without requiring to adjust the kernel.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim the paper attributes to Ref. 12 (Agliardi et al.).
assertions.reader_inference: Ref. 12 is not run as a baseline here, so the claimed advantage over it is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ref. 13, that quantum kernels were shown superior to classical kernels for anomaly detection in high energy physics.
quotes: Ref [13] demonstrates the superiority of quantum kernels over classical kernels for anomaly detection in high energy physics.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 13 (Belis et al.).
